title: Saraband
full_review:
Older filmgoers may remember the big splash made by Ingmar Bergman's "Scenes from a Marriage" -- a television series, but released theatrically in a shortened version -- in 1973.
Stars Liv Ullmann and Erland Josephson were fabulous in that groundbreaking look at a fractious relationship.

And now, all these years later, Bergman has come up with a somber but intelligent sequel, "Saraband" (Sony Pictures Classics) -- divided into 10 "chapters" -- that has Marianne (Ullmann), a lawyer, paying a surprise visit to the husband, Johan (Josephson), she divorced 32 years ago. (He's not exactly pleased when she shows up.)

She becomes embroiled in the tensions between Johan and his estranged conductor son, Henrik (Borje Ahlstedt), and aspiring cellist granddaughter, Karin (Julia Dufvenius), both of whom live in Johan's guesthouse.

As you might expect from the great Bergman, the drama features predictably superb, beautifully nuanced work from his actors. Ullmann is as expressive as ever, and Josephson is totally convincing in his role as a rather unlikable character.

He even has a brief nude scene when he experiences a nocturnal crisis, and comes to Ullmann's room asking if he can sleep with her (for consolation, not sex). He removes his nightshirt, and she removes her clothing. She's mostly in shadows, but the sight of his frail body seems to speak poignantly about his character.

But even with the serious moral themes at work here, the talky film is heavy going and there's even a vaguely incestuous undercurrent between Henrik and Karin, both of whom are in mourning for their wife and mother, Anna, who died two years before. (They even sleep -- chastely, one assumes -- in the same bed.)

The bitter hatred between Johan and Henrik is ugly business indeed -- Henrik wishes his father would die a horrible death -- and even the generally sympathetic Marianne is perhaps less than admirable. (She has an institutionalized daughter whom she never sees.)

Which is not to say that characters can't show sides of themselves that are less than noble, but in this instance the negative is wearying and, though no doubt intentional on Bergman's part, painful to watch.

Bergman's technique is as masterful as ever, as exemplified by his telling use of sounds: a creaking door, footsteps, a ticking clock, and he has stated that this film is his big-screen swan song. Despite all its faults, serious film buffs will want to catch this.

This film, with subtitles, contains profanity and crude language, brief domestic violence, attempted suicide and brief full-frontal nudity. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
